result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.k_components()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find the k-component structure of the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L40977-L41053){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.k_components() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![k-components](/assets/graphs/k-components.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The shared eight-node core graph: a dense cluster A, B, C, D, a ring through E, F, G, and a pendant H. The whole graph is the 1-component (gray); dropping H, which hangs on a single cut vertex, leaves A to G, the 2-component (teal); and the cluster A, B, C, D survives the loss of any two nodes, so it is the 3-component (accent). The table lists the components at each level k." width="100%"} A k-component is a maximal subset of nodes such that every pair of nodes in the subset has node connectivity at least k. The result is a dictionary mapping each connectivity level k to the list of k-components at that level. For directed graphs, k-connectivity means that removing any fewer than k nodes keeps the induced subgraph strongly connected. This extends the standard undirected k-components to digraphs. The k-components form a hierarchical structure: every (k+1)-component is contained within some k-component. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, list[list[int]]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A dictionary where keys are connectivity levels k (positive integers) and values are lists of k-components (each component is a list of node IDs). ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Uses the Moody-White cohesive blocking approach: 1. **Base case (k=1):** strongly connected components (directed) or connected components (undirected). 2. **Recursion:** for each component, compute its vertex connectivity $\kappa$. If $\kappa > k$, the component is also a $(k+1)$-, ..., $\kappa$-component. Then find minimum vertex separators and recurse on the resulting sub-components to find higher-connectivity subsets. For directed graphs, vertex connectivity between an ordered pair $(u, v)$ is the maximum number of internally vertex-disjoint directed paths from $u$ to $v$. The algorithm checks both directions for every pair. Complexity is dominated by pairwise max-flow computations: $O(n^2)$ max-flow calls per component, each $O(VE)$. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A triangle with one pendant node: the whole graph is a 1-component, and the triangle on its own is a 2-component: ::: {#52cff480 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("C", "D")]) ) kc = graph.k_components() sorted(kc.keys()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [1, 2] ``` ::: ::: A complete directed graph on 4 nodes is 3-connected: ::: {#fa68ee03 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(directed=True) for n in ["A", "B", "C", "D"]: g.add_node(label=n) for s in ["A", "B", "C", "D"]: for t in ["A", "B", "C", "D"]: if s != t: g.add_edge(s, t) kc = g.k_components() max(kc.keys()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 3 ``` ::: :::
